blocks.text: The Egyptians assert that vultures mark out the place of a battle not three days but seven days beforehand, and that they even foresee on which side the greater slaughter will be. Horus, Hieroglyphics book 1, chapter 11: Πολέμου μέλλοντος τελειοῦσθαι, τὸν τόπον ὁρίζει, ἐν ᾧ μέλλει ὁ πόλεμος γίνεσθαι, πρὸ ἡμέρων ἑπτὰ ἐπ' αὐτὸν παραγινομένη· [polemou mellontos teleiousthai, ton topon horizei, en hō mellei ho polemos ginesthai, pro hēmerōn hepta ep' auton paraginomenē] When the time for waging a war is at hand, it marks out the place in which the battle is to be joined, coming to it seven days beforehand. And again: Πλείονας σφαζομένους, καὶ ἡττωμένους, βλέπει, ταμιευομένη τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἐκ τῶν πτωμάτων τροφήν· παρ' ὃ καὶ οἱ ἀρχαῖοι βασιλεῖς κατασκόπους ἔπεμπον σκεπτομένους κατὰ ποῖον τοῦ πολέμου οἱ γῦπες βλέπουσι μέρος, ἐντεῦθεν σημειούμενοι τοὺς ἡττωμένους. [pleionas sphazomenous, kai hēttōmenous, blepei, tamieuomenē tēn heautou ek tōn ptōmatōn trophēn; par' ho kai hoi archaioi basileis kataskopous epempon skeptomenous kata poion tou polemou hoi gypes blepousi meros, enteuthen sēmeioumenoi tous hēttōmenous] It foresees where more are to be slain, and who are to be defeated, so as to set aside food for itself from the corpses. Accordingly the ancient kings used to send out scouts to observe towards which part of the battle line the vultures were looking, and to infer from this who were to be defeated. These things, as being at least partly true, are greatly marvelled at by those Fathers who wrote on the Hexaemeron. Basil, Homily 8: Τίς τοῖς γυψὶ προαπαγγέλλων τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὸν θάνατον, ὅταν κατ' ἀλλήλων ἐπιστρατεύσωσιν; ἴδοις γὰρ ἂν μυρίας ἀγέλας γυπῶν τοῖς στρατοπέδοις παρεπομένας, ἐκ τῆς τῶν ὅπλων παρασκευῆς τεκμαιρομένων τὴν ἔκβασιν. [tis tois gypsi proapangellōn tōn anthrōpōn ton thanaton, hotan kat' allēlōn epistrateusōsin? idois gar an myrias agelas gypōn tois stratopedois parepomenas, ek tēs tōn hoplōn paraskeuēs tekmairomenōn tēn ekbasin] Ambrose rendered this as follows: I will ask you, and you answer me: How is it that vultures are accustomed to announce the death of men by certain signs? By what indication have they been taught and instructed that, when opposing armies begin a lamentable war against each other, these birds follow in a great flock, having foretold it, and thereby signify that a multitude of men will fall in the war, to become prey for the vultures? And Eustathius: Ἡνίκα δέ φασιν ἄνδρες εἰς πόλεμον παρατάσσονται, ἐπακολουθεῖ αὐτοῖς, καὶ οὐκ ἀφίσταται, σαρκοβόρος ὤν· [hēnika de phasin andres eis polemon paratassontai, epakolouthei autois, kai ouk aphistatai, sarkoboros ōn] But when men are drawn up in battle array, it follows and does not depart, since it is greedy for flesh. Hence legacy hunters are compared to vultures. In this sense Seneca says in Epistle 95: He is a vulture, he is waiting for a corpse. And Martial, book 6, Epigram 62:
